newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia defence chief sees no threat from China.
newsitem.headline: Australia defence chief sees no threat from China.

text.p: Australian armed forces chief General John Baker said on Wednesday that China was unlikely to pose a military threat to the Asian region and would instead focus on economic growth.
"If you want economic development, you get that in times of peace and stability, not in times of conflict, and I expect China will act accordingly," Baker told the National Press Club.
"I think their main trade and economic opportunities will continue to be their dominant priority, not expansion of Chinese hegemony," Baker said.
Baker said Australia and the United States now had a chance to encourage China to take its place as a major world power.

Beijing has expressed concern that Australia and the United States are conducting an undeclared policy of containing China through stronger defence ties, but both Canberra and U.S. President Bill Clinton in recent weeks have rejected the charge.

Baker warned there would always be areas of disagreement between the three countries. "I don't think we will ever reach the stage where we will be in complete agreement with China on every issue," he said.
"What's important is that the bulk of the relationship over-rides the small differences that will exist from time to time and I am confident that we can achieve that."
Baker also said he expected China and the United States to gradually move towards a closer security relationship.
In a sign of improving relations between Washington and Beijing, the Pentagon announced on Monday that Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian will visit the United States next month.

On Sunday, Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin agreed on a framework for summit talks over the next two years, starting with a visit to China by U.S. Vice President Al Gore in the first part of 1997.

"I think that China and America...need to engage in the sort of strategic dialogue that we are engaging in and I see every sign of that happening because of the Chinese visits to America and vice versa," Baker said.

"I am confident that in due course we will develop a very interesting, a very informative and a very valuable strategic dialogue with China -- all for the good and all for peace and stability, not for conflict."
But concerns about China's strategic intentions have been growing in the Asian region, particularly in relation to disputes over the Spratly Islands in the South China Sea.
Singapore Defence Minister Tony Tan warned in October that territorial claims over the Spratlys could result in conflict and disruption to navigational freedom.

China is one of six nations laying claim to all or part of the islands. The others are Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam and Taiwan. China has also sparked regional unrest over a range of other territorial claims.
